title: Outcome Measures, Documentation, Consent and Referral
lead: Measure what matters, write it clearly, act safely.

book.title: Outcome Measures, Documentation, Consent and Referral
book.lead: Measure what matters, write it clearly, act safely.

blocks.text: Without measurement, neither you nor the patient can tell whether treatment is working. Outcome measures turn "I feel a bit better" into data that guide decisions.

rows: Neck Disability Index, Oswestry Disability Index, QuickDASH, KOOS, LEFS
Daily function for that body region
Timed Up and Go, 30-second sit-to-stand, 6-minute walk test, grip strength
What the patient can actually do
STarT Back Tool, Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire, Tampa Scale

blocks.text: The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) is the smallest change patients consider meaningful. Quote MCID values only from verified sources [Ref – to verify].

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: Choose at least one self-report measure and one performance measure for every patient. Self-report tells you how the patient experiences the change; performance tells you what changed objectively.

items: Weak: "Improve walking."
SMART: "Walk 500 metres to the mosque without stopping, with pain no more than 3/10, within 4 weeks."

rows: Patient report, body chart summary, behaviour, flags screened
"R buttock to post knee ache 6/10, worse sitting 20 min. Red flags screened: nil."
"Lumbar flexion fingertips to mid-shin reproduces leg pain. SLR R 50° reproduces post thigh pain. Neuro: intact."
"Somatic referred pain from lumbar spine likely. Hip less likely: hip exam normal."
Treatment given, dose, response, home program, next review
"Repeated extension in lying 10 reps: leg pain reduced to 3/10. HEP: 10 reps every 2 hours. Review 1 week."

blocks.text: Record what you screened for, what you found, what you decided and why. If you refer, record to whom, how urgently and what you told the patient.

blocks.label: COMMON STUDENT TRAP
body: "Patient fine, continue treatment" is not documentation. If it is not written, legally and professionally it did not happen.

blocks.text: Before examination and treatment, the patient must understand and agree. Explain in plain language:

items: What you propose to do and why.
What the patient will feel and any common side effects (for example temporary soreness).
Material risks, especially for higher-risk techniques such as cervical manipulation.
Reasonable alternatives, including no treatment.
That the patient may stop or withdraw consent at any time.

blocks.text: Offer a chaperone for intimate or sensitive examinations, respect cultural and religious preferences regarding gender of the therapist and exposure, and document consent. Follow AHPC and local regulations.

sections.title: 5.5 Referral decisions and writing a referral

rows: Suspected cauda equina syndrome, acute coronary syndrome, stroke
Stop, arrange emergency transfer, phone ahead if possible, document time
Suspected fracture, progressive neurological deficit, suspected malignancy
Direct contact with a physician, written referral, safety-net advice to patient
Persisting symptoms despite adequate care, need for injection or surgical opinion

items: Patient identifiers and date.
Reason for referral in one sentence at the top.
Key findings: history, examination, red flags present and absent.
What you have done and the response.
Your specific question ("Please assess for possible cervical myelopathy").
Urgency and your contact details.

blocks.label: CLINICAL CASE
body: Referral sentence example: "I would be grateful for your urgent review of Mr A, 62, who presents with 6 weeks of bilateral hand numbness, clumsiness and a positive Hoffmann sign, suggesting possible cervical myelopathy. Manual therapy has not been started."

blocks.text: Always tell patients what new symptoms should make them seek help urgently, and how. For example: "If you develop numbness between your legs or problems passing urine, go to the emergency department immediately." Document that safety-net advice was given.

items: **Why include a performance measure?** It captures objective change that self-report may miss, and it may change at a different rate.
**Rewrite "reduce pain" as a SMART goal.** "Reduce worst daily neck pain from 7/10 to 3/10 or less during an 8-hour working day within 6 weeks."
**What must you document when you refer urgently?** The findings, the urgency, the person contacted, the time, and what the patient was told.
**A patient refuses a test you think is important. What do you do?** Explain why it matters, respect the decision, document the refusal and its implications, and adjust your plan.
**What is safety-netting?** Giving clear instructions about which warning symptoms require urgent help and what to do.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Select appropriate outcome measures for a patient.
Write SMART goals and SOAP notes.
Obtain and document informed consent.
Choose the correct urgency of referral and write a clear referral letter.
